strengths: Combining BORE-style class-probability acquisition with label propagation or label spreading is a coherent, potentially useful contribution, particularly when a finite candidate pool supplies geometry without additional objective evaluations. The relationship to BORE, LFBO, and established semi-supervised methods is clearly acknowledged.

The experiments cover synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and image-derived search, with ten repetitions. Several plots show substantial improvements over GP acquisitions and multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers, especially on synthetic and NATS-Bench tasks.

The supplementary ablations examine kernel parameters, unlabeled-point counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. Including a comparator without transductive learning provides useful evidence that unlabeled points can improve the proposed kernel-based approach.
weaknesses: The theoretical conclusions in Section 4.3 are not established for the proposed algorithm. Equations (11)–(13) invoke minimax and existence results involving oracle knowledge of decision sets, but do not show that the implemented label propagation/spreading methods satisfy those results or that the required separation between error bounds holds here. Classification-risk bounds also do not directly establish acquisition quality or optimization regret. Consequently, the claim following Equation (8) that the classifier is better than or equivalent to other classifiers is unsupported.

The sampling justification does not establish the central mechanism. Truncated Gaussian sampling around evaluated points does not enforce Assumption 4.1: high-density paths can cross objective-induced class boundaries, which themselves change with the threshold. In this setting, generated points provide an inductive bias rather than independent information about an unknown input distribution. Neither guaranteed expansion of the favorable decision region nor its connection to improved exploration is demonstrated.

The experimental protocol omits consequential details, including the main benchmark values or selection procedures for beta and alpha, feature scaling and categorical encoding, pool subsample sizes, and acquisition maximization over discrete pools. These omissions matter especially because Figure s.4 shows pronounced kernel-parameter sensitivity. A smaller, correctable issue is that Section 4.1's elementwise transition probabilities normalize columns, whereas the stated matrix expression normalizes rows.

The evidence does not adequately isolate the claimed resolution of overconfidence. The paper defines overconfidence through concentration of favorable predictions, but does not quantify this property or connect it systematically to optimization outcomes. The no-transduction ablation is useful but limited to two functions. Controls for the random tie-breaking heuristic and matched supervised smoothing or regularization would help distinguish competing explanations. Random search is absent, and the meaning of the plotted uncertainty bands is unspecified.

The scope of the empirical conclusions needs qualification. Continuous optimization with generated unlabeled points is tested only on two-dimensional functions. The MNIST experiment uses embeddings trained on 440,000 images with the exact three-digit labels that determine the optimization objective. Although training and test splits are separate, this substantial objective-aligned supervision limits its value as evidence for high-dimensional black-box optimization; ranking candidates directly with the pretrained classifier is an important missing comparison.

Practical efficiency remains unverified. Dense graph construction and propagation, together with 1,000 acquisition-optimization initializations, can introduce considerable overhead, but no runtime or memory comparisons are reported. Pool-size sensitivity experiments on small synthetic problems do not establish scalability on the much larger application pools. The promising optimization curves therefore support substantive merit, but the theoretical and experimental gaps make acceptance premature.
